ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the gods
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The gods are not explained here. The colony learns of them the way its people do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: The colony's own book of the gods is a tab of the region window: what its people saw, were told and believe.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Nobody explains the gods, and this Almanac doesn't either. Your colonists will see things, hear the old stories from visitors and neighbors, argue about what they mean, and sometimes be wrong; what they saw, were told and believe is written in the colony's own book of the gods, a tab of the region window. One setting, under The gods on the What's on page, decides whether the gods are there at all. No setting changes how plainly they show themselves: most of the time nobody can be sure what a god did, and now and then one shows itself plainly.
What the colony's own people do for their gods is plain, though. Any altar, ritual place, sculpture or shrine of the colony's can be given to a god the colony knows (its button, Dedicate to a god): someone walks over and says the words, and a card says what the colony's people will do there from then on. They leave a small gift there now and then from what the stores can spare (a packed-away sculpture too, never one on show), come to pray there in hard times, and keep the god's feast day there. What they carry on their own is only what the colony has plenty of and can make or gather again; something precious to it (components, medicine past herbal, gold, plasteel, glitterworld goods, anything it can't make yet) goes only when someone devout asks you first, on a card with Yes and No, and then they carry it themselves. The book keeps every gift, where it was left and what became of it, and in each god's chapter its keeper's reading of how that god stands toward the colony, in words only, as the keeper reads it. The place's inspect line shows what was last left there, what became of it, and what someone here holds the god loves; what becomes of a gift is what anyone can see where it lay (gone by morning, something else found in its place, or still lying there), and whoever finds it says whose doing they take it for. A prayer gives a small good mood, a little more said at the god's own place, and carrying a gift a small one for a day. On the night of the Open Door, where the colony keeps it, the cook sets a bowl on the table at dusk for whoever comes in the night. In the book, a god's chapter opens with what the colony takes it to be, the colony's own sign of it drawn beside its name, once someone has told what it is; the same sign is on a god's card when the colony is sure who it was. Some of what they do comes of their own accord, in the moments that call for it: someone sits up the night with one of the frail in a hard cold snap, some of them walk to the well at dusk in a long dry spell and sing down into it, the colony walks out together on a feast day to eat the year's first fruit in the noon sun, someone presses a few coins into a visitor's hand, someone stands at the door looking out on a night with no moon, someone sits up all night with one of the colony fighting a craving. What came of it, if anything, is told as it was seen.
Each god's feast day has a custom of its own, kept the way the feast's own words say, once its letter is answered: saplings set by hand for the trees the colony has felled and a meal eaten under its oldest tree; silver carried from the stores and dropped down into the rock; the herd walked out to the long grass at the edge and an old story told to the children at dusk; the year's scraps dug into a field and a pot of mushroom stew cooked from the stores; something broken mended, the machines looked over and every lamp left lit through the night; a silent supper of the plainest food with the sick and the old seated nearest the fire; the doors to the outside shut and every lamp lit at nightfall, put back as they were at dawn; a watch on the walls till dawn and dreams told at breakfast. Those who hold the god go first, and at the feast's rite they stand behind the one leading it. What was done is told when it is done, and kept in the book. Some animals your colonists hold to be a god's, each by their own reading, and they may be wrong. One of the colony's own they greet the first time, bring a bite by hand now and then, feed first and walk to the god's place on its feast day, and grieve a little when it dies; one born on that feast day is an omen. A wild beast that stays may be taken for a god's when it is named, and then the council's question about it has their answer first, to leave it be. A rare beast on the land (with PokéWorld, its legendaries) may be taken for a god's the same way, and hunting one troubles those who believe it. The colony's sculptures may show these moments, as they show any of the colony's stories: someone before a god as the colony knew it, a festival kept, a beast given its name, the herd's old leader dying, a raid held at a line, a season someone took for a god's doing. Now and then a drink or a dose from the stores does more than it should, for good or ill, and nothing about it shows beforehand; what it did is told as it was seen, and the one who took it comes to believe something about it, as the book keeps it.
Each of your colonists holds the gods their own way. Who they are draws them toward one or another (their nature, the work they love, what they are, their past, the people they came from), never their family; praying, carrying gifts, keeping vows and feast days and what they see with their own eyes make it stronger, and neglect, unanswered prayers and broken vows wear it down. They pray to the god they hold most, and the devoted keep a small rite of their own for it now and then, a few seconds and a sentence. Two who hold gods set against each other may bicker about it. Something they saw can win someone over to another god, or leave them afraid of one; the afraid keep away from its place. A colonist's Culture tab says, in words, how they hold each god the colony has heard of and since when; in the book, a god's chapter says who here holds to it and who dreads it, as its keeper writes it down. What someone sees of the gods stays with them by what they hold: a believer is glad of a kindness and comforted, someone who dreads a god is afraid when something of it comes near, someone with no strong belief is awed by a sight or a little uneasy at a sign, and a scoffer shrugs; their mood and their heart show it. Whatever comes after, a small thing most often and a great one rarely, is told as it was seen, and the same thing seldom comes back soon. Many of the strange things people see leave something real behind every time, small but there to be found whether or not anyone saw it happen: a body left lying rots away inside its ring of mushrooms and the ground there turns rich, frost on a grave lets the dead one's closest sleep well, thunder under a clear sky brings rain later that day, a coin found at someone's feet is a real coin.
Your people also keep saints. With Ideology, a faith's deities are its saints (or its damned, feared and never prayed to): the ideoligion screen calls them by the faith's own word for them (saints, ancestors, exemplars, the damned), and in play a line under them names the god each is held to belong to, once your colony knows that god; the faith itself is never changed. When one of your colonists dies a remarkable death (carrying the wounded out of a fight, holding the line to the last, years of tending the sick, years of devotion, a vow kept to the end), the council may be asked to name them a saint of the colony's own: the person, never their family. Their grave, any statue you raise to a saint (its button, Raise to a saint) and the relic set aside when they are named are places the devoted go to pray now and then, and each year, on the day they died, the devoted keep their day at the grave. A god's chapter in the book lists the saints held to be its own.
The gods also reach into your colonists' everyday lives. One who vowed a pilgrimage walks out to a holy place of their god in the region when there is one within a few days' road (a town of a people that holds it, the pilgrim fellowship's shrine, an old shrine by a landmark), and is away as a caravan of their own; home again, they bring something of the place and tell one of that people's stories at supper. A fisher who holds to the god of the waters gives the first fish of the morning back to the water, and fishes better for the rest of the day. The keeper of the colony's book walks out to see a sign they missed, and in the evening sits at a writing table (a writer's table, if you have Vanilla Books Expanded) to write up the new entries. At a eulogy, the speaker gives the dead to the god they held, and those who share that god take the loss a little more easily. Raiders call on their own gods as they come at your walls, and a prisoner may tell their warden a story of their people's gods. When a season goes down in the weather book by a name, your believers say which god sent it, and argue about it if they disagree; when that season comes round again, the council may be asked to keep a day against it. Once the book has a chapter for a god, the room planner offers a shrine room built the way your people picture that god. With Vanilla Christmas Expanded, midwinter brings the festive tree switched on, gingerbread and warm drinks set out, a present for each of your people and a snow sculpture.
